progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: insulin from beta cells; insulin binds receptors and moves glucose transporters into the membrane of muscle and fat cells; the liver stores and releases glucose; usual fasting range about 4 to 6 mmol/L. From b08: insulin resistance ("insulin still binds, but fewer transporters move"), body fat around the liver and organs, beta cells covering then falling behind, high glucose damaging vessels in the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart; risk factor. From b10: rates (not used directly). From b11 (watched before g01 and b12 in the recommended order): randomised controlled trial, "chance decides the groups, so other differences even out". From Year 11: haemoglobin in red blood cells. Not assumed: management, treatment, monitoring (as defined terms), metformin, HbA1c, escalation, remission, placebo, GLP-1, future direction.
progression.startsWith: If type 2 diabetes means cells respond poorly to insulin, why isn't the treatment simply more insulin? Early on, many people with type 2 make plenty of insulin, sometimes more than usual. Adding more of a signal the cells are already ignoring isn't the first move. So how can type 2 diabetes be managed?
progression.stopsAfter: distinguishing type 1 (beta cells destroyed, little or no insulin) from type 2 (insulin present, cells respond poorly, beta cells later fall behind); stating management's two jobs (glucose towards range, lower complication risk); distinguishing management, treatment and monitoring; explaining how activity (contracting muscle moves transporters without insulin) and weight loss (less fat in and around the liver and organs, better response to insulin) act on the cause, and their limit (keeping it up; cost and access); explaining metformin (less glucose released by the liver, better response; cheap, rarely causes low glucose, weight-neutral; doesn't remove resistance; gut side effects); explaining HbA1c (glucose sticks to haemoglobin over a red cell's life, so it averages two to three months; evidence, not treatment); explaining escalation and why insulin manages the consequence (replaces the signal, doesn't restore sensitivity, can add weight); explaining complication care (blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney, eye and foot checks); evaluating management evidence with DiRECT (randomised, large gap at one year; remission faded with weight regain; who was studied; trial against everyday results); evaluating GLP-1 based drugs as a future direction; applying this to a rising HbA1c and to unseen trial evidence.
progression.nextLesson: how prevention campaigns can reduce disease (bio-m8-b13).

teaching.task: If type 2 diabetes means cells respond poorly to insulin, why isn't the treatment just more insulin? How can type 2 diabetes be managed?
teaching.causalExplanation: Earlier, you saw how type 2 develops. In muscle and fat cells, insulin still binds, but fewer glucose transporters reach the membrane, so glucose stays in the blood. The liver also releases too much glucose. Beta cells cover by releasing more insulin, until they fall behind. Type 1 is different: immune cells destroy the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made. Think of insulin as a key. Type 1 has no key. In type 2, the key fits, but the lock is jammed. So management has two jobs. Bring blood glucose back towards its usual range, and lower the risk of damage to blood vessels, kidneys, eyes and nerves. Management is the long-term work of keeping a disease under control, without curing it. A treatment acts on the disease mechanism. And monitoring measures whether the plan is working. A good plan links every action back to the mechanism. Start with lifestyle, because it acts on the cause. When muscles contract during activity, they move glucose transporters into the membrane without needing insulin, so glucose leaves the blood. Losing weight shrinks the fat stored in and around the liver and other organs, so cells respond to insulin better again. The catch is keeping it up for years, which depends on time, money and access to healthy food.
teaching.conversationalApproach: If type 2 diabetes means cells respond poorly to insulin, why isn't the treatment simply more insulin? Early on, many people with type 2 make plenty of insulin, sometimes more than usual. Earlier, you saw how type 2 develops. So management has two jobs. Start with lifestyle, because it acts on the cause. Most people also take a tablet called metformin. How do you know the plan's working? One glucose reading only shows that moment. If HbA1c stays above target, the plan steps up: another medicine, and if beta cells keep falling behind, insulin. How strong is the evidence? Take DiRECT, a trial in Scotland and England. Now judge it. The syllabus also asks about future research. Two exam questions. HbA1c shows average glucose over two to three months, so a rise from 7. Second. It was randomised, with a placebo, so the bigger fall is most likely the drug's effect, and 1. So, for any management question.
teaching.openingDecision: If type 2 diabetes means cells respond poorly to insulin, why isn't the treatment simply more insulin? Early on, many people with type 2 make plenty of insulin, sometimes more than usual. Adding more of a signal the cells are already ignoring isn't the first move. So how can type 2 diabetes be managed?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A person with type 2 diabetes has used metformin and an activity plan for two years. Their HbA1c has risen from 7.0 to 8.4 per cent, and their doctor suggests adding insulin. Explain what the HbA1c result shows, and assess whether insulin alone would fix the underlying problem. Pause here to answer. Second. In a trial, 600 adults with type 2 diabetes were randomly given a new weekly injection or a placebo for 26 weeks. HbA1c fell by 1.4 points with the drug and 0.3 with the placebo. One in eight stopped the drug because of nausea, and it isn't subsidised yet. Evaluate this evidence for using the drug to manage type 2 diabetes. Pause here to answer.

design.visualSystem: One management board. A coded mechanism strip owns the bottom fifth of the frame from scene 3 to scene 7: four slots in mechanism order, "glucose released by liver", "insulin signal", "glucose into muscle and fat cells", "damage to vessels" (b07's PathwayStrip, four-slot mode). Each action docks a small chip into the slot it acts on (lifestyle into slots 2 and 3, metformin into 1 and 2, insulin into 2 only, complication care into 4), and the monitoring meter sits beside the strip, never in a slot, which carries the point that monitoring is not treatment. Above the strip, one painted plate or matched pair at a time with callouts. From scene 8, the strip is replaced by an evidence frame: four slots, "mechanism", "evidence (design, size, length, outcome)", "durability", "access and cost" (the same component), which refills for DiRECT (9), GLP-1 drugs (10) and attempt 2 (11d). No people, hands or faces: lifestyle is shown by organs, transporter plates and plain objects (walking shoes, a vegetable bowl), trials as coded group bars and dot fields. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
design.transitionPlan: no people. the board clears. the columns clear. new m8-walking-shoes-v1. the lifestyle plates shrink and dim. the board clears above the strip. on "steps up" a coded three-step staircase writes at the upper left: "lifestyle + metformin", "add another medicine" (grey tag "for example SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 drugs"), "insulin"; gloss "escalation: the plan steps up". the mechanism strip slides down and away; b07's PathwayStrip writes at the bottom as the evidence frame, four slots: "mechanism", "evidence: design, size, length, outcome", "durability", "access and cost". the bars shrink to the upper left. the board clears; the evidence frame stays, emptied. the board clears. the card stays; a small HbA1cMeter sits beside it. the board clears. the card stays; the evidence frame returns small beside it, empty. the mechanism strip and the evidence frame stack full width, each lighting slot by slot on its cue, with small thumbnails (the jammed KeyLock in "insulin signal"; the DiRECT bars in "evidence"). > Here are the key notes.
